name: Trapezius
etymology: From Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapeza, table), source of ‘trapezium/trapezoid’. Left and right trapezius together form a big trapezoid (four-sided diamond) shape over the upper back.
origin: External occipital protuberance, medial third of superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae, spinous processes of C7–T12
insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion and spine of scapula
actions: Cervical extension and contralateral rotation (upper fibres)
innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
tip: Upper and lower traps form a force couple with serratus anterior for upward rotation — essential for pain-free overhead pressing.

name: Upper trapezius (descending part)
etymology: Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapezoid shape); ‘descending’ because its fibres descend from the skull and neck down to the shoulder.
origin: External occipital protuberance, medial third of superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae
insertion: Lateral third of clavicle
innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
tip: Often overactive and tight (shrugging during presses, desk posture); cue ‘shoulders down’ and strengthen lower trap to rebalance.

name: Middle trapezius (transverse part)
etymology: Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapezoid shape); ‘transverse’ from Latin transversus ‘turned across’ — its fibres run horizontally across from the spine to the scapula.
origin: Spinous processes and supraspinous ligaments of C7–T3 (approximately)
insertion: Medial border of acromion and superior lip of spine of scapula
actions: Stabilises scapula against chest wall during arm movements
innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
tip: Train with prone T-raises and wide-grip rows with a deliberate squeeze of the shoulder blades.

name: Lower trapezius (ascending part)
etymology: Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapezoid shape); ‘ascending’ because its fibres ascend from the lower thoracic spine up to the scapular spine.
origin: Spinous processes and supraspinous ligaments of T4–T12 (approximately)
insertion: Medial end (tubercle) of spine of scapula
innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
tip: Commonly weak in scapular dyskinesis and shoulder impingement — prone Y-raises are the classic strengthening drill.

name: Latissimus dorsi
etymology: From Latin latissimus ‘widest’ (superlative of latus, broad) + dorsi ‘of the back’ (dorsum). So it means ‘the widest muscle of the back’ — the broadest muscle sheet in the body.
origin: Spinous processes of T7–T12, thoracolumbar fascia, posterior iliac crest, lower 3–4 ribs, often the inferior angle of scapula
insertion: Floor of intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
innervation: Thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8)
tip: Prime mover in pull-ups, lat pulldowns and the swimming stroke; tight lats limit overhead reach and pull the lumbar spine into extension when arms go overhead.

name: Rhomboid major
etymology: From Greek rhombos ‘rhombus / spinning top’ + eidos ‘shape’, via Latin; major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger rhombus-shaped muscle’ — a flat parallelogram between spine and scapula.
origin: Spinous processes of T2–T5 and supraspinous ligaments
insertion: Medial border of scapula, from root of spine to inferior angle
innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve (C4–C5)
tip: Works with middle trap in rows; weakness lets the scapula ‘wing’ at its medial border and drift into protraction.

name: Rhomboid minor
etymology: From Greek rhombos ‘rhombus’ + eidos ‘shape’; minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller rhombus-shaped muscle’, sitting just above rhomboid major.
origin: Ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7–T1
insertion: Medial border of scapula at the root (base) of the scapular spine
innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve (C4–C5)
tip: Functionally identical to rhomboid major — trained with rows, face pulls and scapular retraction drills.

name: Levator scapulae
etymology: From Latin levator ‘lifter’ (levare, to raise) + scapulae ‘of the shoulder blade’. So it means ‘the lifter of the scapula’ — exactly what it does.
origin: Transverse processes of C1–C4 (posterior tubercles of C3–C4)
insertion: Medial border of scapula from superior angle to root of spine
actions: Cervical ipsilateral lateral flexion and rotation
innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and cervical nerves C3–C4
tip: Classic source of ‘knot’ pain at the superior angle of the scapula; stretch with neck flexion + contralateral rotation (nose to opposite armpit).

name: Serratus posterior superior
etymology: From Latin serratus ‘saw-toothed’ (serra, saw) + posterior ‘behind’ + superior ‘upper’. So it means ‘the upper saw-toothed muscle at the back’ — its tooth-like slips attach to the ribs.
origin: Ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7–T3
insertion: Superior borders of ribs 2–5, lateral to their angles
innervation: Intercostal nerves T2–T5
tip: A thin respiratory muscle under the rhomboids; its role is debated and it is often blamed in vague upper-back pain.

name: Serratus posterior inferior
etymology: From Latin serratus ‘saw-toothed’ (serra, saw) + posterior ‘behind’ + inferior ‘lower’. So it means ‘the lower saw-toothed muscle at the back’, with tooth-like slips to the lowest ribs.
origin: Spinous processes of T11–L2 and thoracolumbar fascia
insertion: Inferior borders of ribs 9–12, near their angles
actions: Depresses and pulls back ribs 9–12 (possibly assists forced expiration or anchors ribs for diaphragm)
innervation: Ventral rami of T9–T12 (lower intercostal and subcostal nerves)
tip: Lies deep to the lats; its true respiratory function is uncertain.

name: Splenius capitis
etymology: From Greek splenion ‘bandage, patch’ + Latin capitis ‘of the head’. So it means ‘the bandage muscle of the head’ — it wraps like a strap over the deeper neck muscles up to the skull.
origin: Lower half of ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7–T3/T4
insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral third of superior nuchal line
innervation: Dorsal rami of middle cervical spinal nerves
tip: Turns the head to the same side, working with the opposite SCM; a common culprit in tension-type neck pain and headaches.

name: Splenius cervicis (colli)
etymology: From Greek splenion ‘bandage, patch’ + Latin cervicis ‘of the neck’ (colli is the TA alternative, from collum, neck). So it means ‘the bandage muscle of the neck’ — the strap stops at the cervical vertebrae, not the skull.
origin: Spinous processes of T3–T6
insertion: Posterior tubercles of transverse processes of C1–C3
innervation: Dorsal rami of lower cervical spinal nerves
tip: Lies just lateral and inferior to splenius capitis; same actions but on the cervical spine instead of the head.

name: Iliocostalis lumborum
etymology: From Latin ilium ‘flank / hip bone’ + costa ‘rib’ + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘the hip-to-rib muscle of the lower back’ — it runs from the iliac crest up to the ribs.
origin: Common erector spinae tendon: iliac crest, sacrum, lumbar spinous processes and thoracolumbar fascia
insertion: Angles of the lower 6–9 ribs (and transverse processes of upper lumbar vertebrae)
innervation: Dorsal rami of lumbar and lower thoracic spinal nerves
tip: The most lateral erector column — the visible ‘ropes’ beside the spine in deadlift lockout; resists side-bending under load.

name: Iliocostalis thoracis
etymology: From Latin ilium ‘hip bone’ + costa ‘rib’ + thoracis ‘of the chest’. Despite the name it runs rib-to-rib — it is the thoracic segment of the ‘hip-to-rib’ column.
origin: Angles of ribs 7–12 (medial to iliocostalis lumborum insertions)
insertion: Angles of ribs 1–6 and transverse process of C7
innervation: Dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves
tip: Helps maintain an upright thoracic posture; part of what keeps the upper back from rounding under load.

name: Iliocostalis cervicis (colli)
etymology: From Latin ilium ‘hip bone’ + costa ‘rib’ + cervicis ‘of the neck’ (colli = of the neck, from collum). The neck segment of the ‘hip-to-rib’ column: it runs from ribs up to the neck.
origin: Angles of ribs 3–6
insertion: Posterior tubercles of transverse processes of C4–C6
innervation: Dorsal rami of cervical and upper thoracic spinal nerves
tip: The uppermost iliocostalis — think of the column as overlapping relay segments climbing from pelvis to neck.

name: Longissimus thoracis
etymology: From Latin longissimus ‘longest’ (superlative of longus) + thoracis ‘of the chest’. So it means ‘the longest muscle, thoracic part’ — longissimus is the longest erector column.
origin: Common erector spinae tendon (sacrum, iliac crest, lumbar spinous processes) and transverse processes of lumbar vertebrae
insertion: Transverse processes of all thoracic vertebrae, ribs 2/3–12 between tubercles and angles, and lumbar accessory processes
innervation: Dorsal rami of thoracic and lumbar spinal nerves
tip: The largest erector column; a key target in back extensions and the hinge pattern, and often guarded/spasmed in acute low back pain.

name: Longissimus cervicis (colli)
etymology: From Latin longissimus ‘longest’ + cervicis ‘of the neck’ (colli, from collum, neck). So it means ‘the longest muscle, neck part’.
origin: Transverse processes of T1–T5 (upper 4–6 thoracic vertebrae)
insertion: Posterior tubercles of transverse processes of C2–C6
innervation: Dorsal rami of lower cervical and upper thoracic spinal nerves
tip: Lies just medial to longissimus capitis; supports the neck in extension and posture.

name: Longissimus capitis
etymology: From Latin longissimus ‘longest’ + capitis ‘of the head’. So it means ‘the longest muscle, head part’ — the only erector column that reaches the skull.
origin: Transverse processes of T1–T4/T5 and articular processes of C4–C7
insertion: Posterior margin of mastoid process of temporal bone
actions: Ipsilateral lateral flexion of head and neck
innervation: Dorsal rami of middle and lower cervical spinal nerves
tip: Lies deep to splenius capitis and shares its mastoid attachment and same-side rotation.

name: Spinalis thoracis
etymology: From Latin spinalis ‘of the spine’ (spina, thorn / spinous process) + thoracis ‘of the chest’. So it means ‘the spinous-process muscle of the chest region’ — it runs spinous process to spinous process.
origin: Spinous processes of T11–L2
insertion: Spinous processes of T1–T8 (upper 4–8 thoracic)
innervation: Dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves
tip: The smallest, most medial erector column — hugs the spinous processes.

name: Spinalis cervicis (colli)
etymology: From Latin spinalis ‘of the spine / spinous processes’ + cervicis ‘of the neck’ (colli, from collum). So it means ‘the spinous-process muscle of the neck’.
origin: Lower ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7–T2
insertion: Spinous process of C2 (axis), sometimes C3–C4
innervation: Dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
tip: Small and inconstant — frequently absent or fused with semispinalis.

name: Spinalis capitis
etymology: From Latin spinalis ‘of the spine / spinous processes’ + capitis ‘of the head’. So it means ‘the spinous-process muscle that reaches the head’.
origin: Spinous processes of C7–T1 (variable; usually arises with semispinalis capitis)
insertion: Occipital bone between superior and inferior nuchal lines (with semispinalis capitis)
innervation: Dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
tip: Usually inseparable from semispinalis capitis and often considered part of it.

name: Semispinalis thoracis
etymology: From Latin semi ‘half’ + spinalis ‘of the spine’ + thoracis ‘of the chest’. Probably named because the semispinalis system covers roughly the upper half of the vertebral column; it runs transverse process to spinous process.
origin: Transverse processes of T6–T10
insertion: Spinous processes of C6–T4 (spanning 4–6 segments)
innervation: Dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves
tip: The most superficial transversospinalis layer; longest fibres (4–6 segments) compared with multifidus (2–4) and rotatores (1–2).

name: Semispinalis cervicis (colli)
etymology: From Latin semi ‘half’ + spinalis ‘of the spine’ + cervicis ‘of the neck’ (colli, from collum). Probably named because it spans the upper ‘half’ of the spine, transverse to spinous processes.
origin: Transverse processes of T1–T6
insertion: Spinous processes of C2–C5 (largest attachment on C2)
innervation: Dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
tip: A major deep neck extensor that stabilises cervical lordosis; part of deep neck extensor training in neck pain rehab.

name: Multifidus lumborum
etymology: From Latin multus ‘many’ + findere ‘to split’ (-fidus, split) + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘split into many parts, of the low back’ — many short bundles fanning between vertebrae.
origin: Dorsal sacrum, posterior superior iliac spine, erector spinae aponeurosis and mammillary processes of lumbar vertebrae
insertion: Spinous processes 2–4 segments above
innervation: Medial branches of dorsal rami of lumbar spinal nerves (each fascicle by the nerve of its own level)
tip: Atrophies and gets fatty infiltration on the painful side in low back pain and does not recover spontaneously — targeted motor-control training is key.

name: Multifidus thoracis
etymology: From Latin multus ‘many’ + -fidus ‘split’ + thoracis ‘of the chest’. So it means ‘split into many parts, of the thoracic region’.
origin: Transverse processes of thoracic vertebrae
insertion: Spinous processes 2–4 segments above
innervation: Medial branches of dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves
tip: Thinner than the lumbar part; contributes to segmental control during thoracic rotation.

name: Multifidus cervicis (colli)
etymology: From Latin multus ‘many’ + -fidus ‘split’ + cervicis ‘of the neck’ (colli, from collum). So it means ‘split into many parts, of the neck’.
origin: Articular processes of C4–C7
insertion: Spinous processes of C2–C5 (2–4 segments above)
innervation: Medial branches of dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
tip: Part of the deep neck extensors that show altered activity and fatty infiltration after whiplash and in chronic neck pain.

name: Rotatores
etymology: From Latin rotator ‘one who turns’ (rotare, to turn, from rota, wheel), plural rotatores. So it means ‘the rotators’ — named for their assumed role in turning the spine.
origin: Transverse processes of vertebrae (best developed in thoracic region)
insertion: Lamina and base of spinous process 1 segment above (brevis) or 2 segments above (longus)
innervation: Medial branches of dorsal rami of spinal nerves
tip: The deepest, shortest transversospinalis layer — rich in muscle spindles, so likely more a position sensor than a rotator.

name: Interspinales lumborum
etymology: From Latin inter ‘between’ + spina ‘thorn / spinous process’ + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘the muscles between the spinous processes of the low back’.
origin: Superior surface of lumbar spinous processes
insertion: Inferior surface of the spinous process immediately above
innervation: Dorsal rami of lumbar spinal nerves
tip: Four or so short pairs either side of the interspinous ligament; mainly sensory/stabilising.

name: Interspinales thoracis
etymology: From Latin inter ‘between’ + spina ‘spinous process’ + thoracis ‘of the chest’. So it means ‘the muscles between the thoracic spinous processes’.
origin: Spinous processes of thoracic vertebrae (usually only at the top, T1–T2, and bottom, T11–T12)
insertion: Spinous process of the adjacent vertebra above
innervation: Dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves
tip: Often absent through the mid-thoracic spine, where the overlapping spinous processes leave little room.

name: Interspinales cervicis (colli)
etymology: From Latin inter ‘between’ + spina ‘spinous process’ + cervicis ‘of the neck’ (colli, from collum). So it means ‘the muscles between the neck’s spinous processes’.
origin: Spinous processes of C3–T1
insertion: Spinous process of the vertebra above (from C2 down), paired either side of the bifid tips
innervation: Dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
tip: Best developed in the neck, where bifid spinous processes give each side its own little muscle.

name: Lateral intertransversarii lumborum (dorsal part)
parts: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles
etymology: From Latin inter ‘between’ + transversus ‘turned across’ (transverse process) + lateralis ‘side’ + dorsalis ‘back’ + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘the back slips of the side muscles between lumbar transverse processes’.
origin: Accessory process of a lumbar vertebra
insertion: Transverse process of the vertebra above
innervation: Ventral rami of lumbar spinal nerves
tip: Tiny segmental muscles — more sensors and stabilisers than movers.

name: Lateral intertransversarii lumborum (ventral part)
parts: Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles
etymology: From Latin inter ‘between’ + transversus ‘turned across’ (transverse process) + lateralis ‘side’ + ventralis ‘belly / front’ + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘the front slips of the side muscles between lumbar transverse processes’.
origin: Transverse process of a lumbar vertebra
insertion: Transverse process of the vertebra above
innervation: Ventral rami of lumbar spinal nerves
tip: Embryologically related to the intercostals, which is why they are supplied by ventral rami.

name: Levatores costarum breves
etymology: From Latin levatores ‘lifters’ (levare, to raise) + costarum ‘of the ribs’ (costa, rib) + breves ‘short’. So it means ‘the short rib-lifters’ — each spans just one segment.
origin: Tips of transverse processes of C7–T11
insertion: Outer surface of the rib immediately below, between tubercle and angle
actions: Ipsilateral lateral flexion and contralateral rotation of thoracic spine (minor)
innervation: Dorsal rami of C8–T11 spinal nerves
tip: Small fan-shaped muscles; mostly of interest for respiration and segmental thoracic mobility.

name: Levatores costarum longi
etymology: From Latin levatores ‘lifters’ + costarum ‘of the ribs’ + longi ‘long’. So it means ‘the long rib-lifters’ — they skip one rib.
origin: Transverse processes of lower thoracic vertebrae (approximately T7–T10)
insertion: Rib two levels below, between tubercle and angle (skipping one rib)
actions: Ipsilateral lateral flexion and contralateral rotation of thoracic spine (minor)
innervation: Dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves
tip: Found only in the lower thorax; the ‘longi’ simply cross two segments instead of one.

name: External intercostals
etymology: From Latin externus ‘outer’ + inter ‘between’ + costa ‘rib’. So it means ‘the outer muscles between the ribs’ — the outermost of three intercostal layers.
origin: Inferior border of the rib above
insertion: Superior border of the rib below; fibres run down and forward (‘hands in pockets’)
innervation: Intercostal nerves (T1–T11)
tip: Fibres run like the external oblique; they are the main intercostal inspiratory layer and work hard in heavy breathing.

name: Internal intercostals
etymology: From Latin internus ‘inner’ + inter ‘between’ + costa ‘rib’. So it means ‘the inner muscles between the ribs’ — the middle intercostal layer, deep to the externals.
origin: Inferior border and costal groove of the rib above
insertion: Superior border of the rib below; fibres run down and back, at right angles to the externals
actions: Rib depression during forced expiration (interosseous part)
innervation: Intercostal nerves (T1–T11)
tip: Active in forced exhalation — e.g. coughing, the end of a hard breath out during bracing or sprinting.

name: Innermost intercostals
etymology: From English ‘innermost’ (Latin intimus, innermost) + inter ‘between’ + costa ‘rib’. So it means ‘the deepest muscles between the ribs’.
origin: Internal surface of the rib above (lateral parts of intercostal spaces)
insertion: Internal surface of the rib below
actions: Likely act with internal intercostals (rib depression in forced expiration)
innervation: Intercostal nerves
tip: Separated from the internal intercostals by the intercostal nerve, artery and vein — which run in the costal groove just under each rib.

name: Transversus thoracis
etymology: From Latin transversus ‘turned across’ + thoracis ‘of the chest’. So it means ‘the transverse muscle of the chest’ — it fans across the inside of the front chest wall.
origin: Posterior surface of lower body of sternum and xiphoid process
insertion: Internal surfaces of costal cartilages 2–6
innervation: Intercostal nerves (T2–T6)
tip: Lies inside the chest wall, continuous below with transversus abdominis — think of it as TrA’s thoracic cousin.

name: Diaphragm
etymology: From Greek dia ‘across, through’ + phragma ‘fence, partition’ (phrassein, to fence in). So it means ‘the partition across’ — the dome-shaped wall between chest and abdomen.
origin: Sternal part: back of xiphoid; costal part: inner surfaces of lower 6 costal cartilages and ribs; lumbar part: crura on L1–L3 bodies and medial/lateral arcuate ligaments
insertion: Central tendon
actions: Inspiration (contracts and descends, enlarging thoracic cavity)
innervation: Phrenic nerve (C3–C5)
tip: ‘C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive’; diaphragmatic (belly) breathing and 360° bracing use it to build intra-abdominal pressure that stabilises the spine.

name: Rectus abdominis
etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the straight muscle of the belly’ — its fibres run straight up and down.
origin: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis
insertion: Xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5–7
innervation: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11) and subcostal nerve (T12)
tip: The ‘six-pack’ comes from tendinous intersections; separation of the two bellies at the linea alba is diastasis recti, common postpartum.

name: External oblique
etymology: From Latin externus ‘outer’ + obliquus ‘slanting’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the outer slanted abdominal muscle’ — its fibres slant down and forward.
origin: External surfaces of ribs 5–12
insertion: Linea alba, pubic tubercle and anterior half of iliac crest (lower edge forms the inguinal ligament)
innervation: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11) and subcostal nerve (T12)
tip: Fibres run ‘hands in pockets’; the right external oblique pairs with the left internal oblique to rotate the trunk to the left.

name: Internal oblique
etymology: From Latin internus ‘inner’ + obliquus ‘slanting’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the inner slanted abdominal muscle’ — fibres slant up and forward, at right angles to the external oblique.
origin: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior two-thirds of iliac crest, lateral half of inguinal ligament
insertion: Inferior borders of ribs 10–12, linea alba, and pubic crest/pecten via conjoint tendon
innervation: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal (T12), iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1)
tip: Rotates to the same side (unlike the external oblique); trained with Pallof presses, cable chops and side planks.

name: Transversus abdominis
etymology: From Latin transversus ‘turned across’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the cross-wise abdominal muscle’ — fibres run horizontally round the belly like a corset.
origin: Internal surfaces of costal cartilages 7–12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lateral third of inguinal ligament
insertion: Linea alba, pubic crest and pecten pubis via conjoint tendon
actions: Tensions thoracolumbar fascia to stabilise lumbar spine and pelvis
innervation: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal (T12), iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1)
tip: The body’s ‘corset’: delayed TrA activation is seen in low back pain; cue drawing-in for isolation, then progress to full bracing for heavy lifts.

name: Pyramidalis
etymology: From Latin pyramidalis ‘pyramid-shaped’ (Greek pyramis, pyramid). So it means ‘the pyramid-shaped muscle’ — a small triangle at the bottom of the rectus sheath, apex pointing up.
origin: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis (anterior to rectus abdominis)
insertion: Linea alba, about halfway to the umbilicus
innervation: Subcostal nerve (T12)
tip: Absent in roughly 10–20% of people; functionally minor.

name: Quadratus lumborum
etymology: From Latin quadratus ‘squared, four-sided’ + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘the square muscle of the low back’ — a rectangular sheet between the 12th rib and the iliac crest.
origin: Posterior iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament
insertion: Medial half of inferior border of 12th rib and transverse processes of L1–L4
actions: Pelvic elevation (‘hip hiking’) on the same side
innervation: Ventral rami of T12–L4
tip: Hikes the hip in gait (and compensates for weak glute med); suitcase carries and side planks train it as a lateral stabiliser.

name: Pubococcygeus
etymology: From Latin pubis (os pubis, pubic bone) + Greek kokkyx ‘cuckoo’ (the coccyx, shaped like a cuckoo’s beak). So it means ‘the pubis-to-coccyx muscle’ — part of the levator ani sling.
origin: Posterior surface of body of pubis and anterior part of tendinous arch of levator ani
insertion: Anococcygeal body (ligament) and coccyx
innervation: Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and pudendal nerve branches (S2–S4)
tip: The ‘PC muscle’ targeted by Kegel exercises; it relaxes as the diaphragm descends and co-contracts with TrA in bracing.

name: Puborectalis (pubo-analis)
etymology: From Latin pubis ‘pubic bone’ + rectum ‘straight (gut)’ / anus ‘ring’. So it means ‘the pubis-to-rectum / anus muscle’ — a U-shaped sling from the pubis around the anorectal junction.
origin: Posterior surface of body of pubis (either side of the symphysis)
insertion: Loops behind the anorectal junction to join its partner; pubo-analis fibres blend into the anal canal wall between the sphincters
innervation: Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and inferior rectal nerve (pudendal, S2–S4)
tip: Paradoxical contraction of this sling during straining is a common cause of obstructed defecation — relaxation training helps.

name: Iliococcygeus
etymology: From Latin ilium ‘flank / hip bone’ + Greek kokkyx ‘cuckoo’ (coccyx, beak-shaped). So it means ‘the hip-bone-to-coccyx muscle’ — though it actually arises from the fascia over obturator internus and the ischial spine, not the ilium itself.
origin: Posterior part of tendinous arch of levator ani (obturator fascia) and ischial spine
insertion: Anococcygeal body and coccyx
innervation: Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and pudendal nerve branches
tip: The thin, flat posterolateral part of levator ani; overstretched in childbirth along with pubococcygeus.

name: Coccygeus
etymology: From Greek kokkyx ‘cuckoo’ — the coccyx resembles a cuckoo’s beak. So it means ‘the coccyx muscle’; the alternative name ischiococcygeus says it runs ischium to coccyx.
origin: Ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament
insertion: Lateral margins of lower sacrum and coccyx
innervation: Ventral rami of S4–S5
tip: Lies on the deep surface of the sacrospinous ligament; can refer pain in coccydynia.

name: External anal sphincter
etymology: From Greek sphinkter ‘that which binds tight’ (sphingein, to bind) + Latin analis ‘of the anus’ (anus, ring) + externus ‘outer’. So it means ‘the outer tightening ring of the anus’.
origin: Perineal body (anteriorly) and skin around anus
insertion: Anococcygeal body and coccyx (posteriorly), encircling the anal canal
actions: Voluntary closure of anal canal (faecal continence)
innervation: Inferior rectal nerve (pudendal, S2–S4) and perineal branch of S4
tip: Voluntary skeletal muscle (unlike the internal sphincter); often injured in obstetric tears, so pelvic floor rehab may target it.
